name: Jamal Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, no problem. I actually like talking about this stuff, my housemates are sick of me going on about it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a carpenter on a timber-frame crew for Northbeam, a firm that builds whole wall panels in a factory and trucks them to site. We crane the panels in, stand them up, bolt and nail them together, then fit the floor cassettes and the roof trusses. On a good day we get the shell of a house up before lunch, which still blows my mind. What wears me out is the crane waiting and the wind, because you can't lift a panel in a strong gust.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology at work now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, honestly. I take a photo of the drawing and ask a chat AI to check the panel order against the plan, and I use it to translate for Andrei, who's from Romania and still learning English. I also use it to sort my budget, which doesn't take long because there isn't much in it. I'm in a shared flat with two other guys and I've got about three weeks' rent saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So AI stays like it is now for me, a handy helper on my phone, and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a good tool, not magic. I'd still tell people on site to use it, because it saves me twenty minutes a day checking drawings. Online I'd probably say the bigger change in building is the factories, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one doesn't really change my job, but the factory side does. I'm already putting up walls that a machine built in a shed, so I know where this goes. Northbeam's factory already has a robot that nails the studs. So even without clever AI, there'll be fewer of us on site in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and try to get a shift or two in the Northbeam factory to learn how the machines work. I'd keep saving, maybe up to a month's rent by summer. And I'd stay in the union, because the factory changes need bargaining whether AI's hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed, to be honest. A bit restless, like I'm waiting for the real change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want a shift in the factory. Has anyone done that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One guy, Liam, moved from site to the factory last year and he says it's warmer and the pay's about the same. They're always short of people who understand how a panel goes together on site. I'd ask my supervisor in January when the work slows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would get in the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mainly. If there's a week between site and factory without pay, I can't afford that. So I'd need it lined up properly before I jump.

say: AI is a **good tool**, not magic, saving him twenty minutes a day on **drawings**.
The bigger change in building comes from **factories**, not AI.
think: **Factory-built panels** already mean fewer site workers in ten years, AI or not.
Northbeam's factory already uses a **robot** to nail the studs.
do: Ask his supervisor in **January** for factory shifts to learn the machines.
Build savings to about **a month's rent** by summer.
Stay in the **union** to bargain over factory changes.
feel: Pretty **relaxed**, but **restless** for the real change.
S0.quote: I'm already putting up walls that a machine built in a shed, so I know where this goes.
fieldNote: Already lives the **automation** story through factory-built panels, so AI hype changes little.
**Uneasy**, not calm: thin savings and few local jobs, plus fewer site workers ahead.
Wants to **move toward the machines**, but can't afford an unpaid gap.

steps.text: Keep using a chat AI to check panel order against drawings
Ask for shifts in the Northbeam panel factory in January
Save up to a month's rent by summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one makes sense to me. The office stuff goes first, the crane and the bolts later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance if workers share in it. I use AI every day to check drawings, and I still want a union in the room when the boss buys the robots. I'd post about that, because the tech isn't the enemy, the deal is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm better placed than most on site because I'm not scared of the tools. But Northbeam would cut the planners and estimators first, and then the pressure comes to fit panels faster. I'd want to be the one who knows the software before they decide who stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd ask Northbeam to put me on the trial when they bring in AI planning, because someone on site has to tell it what's real. I'd do an online course in building information modelling, which is the 3D models builders work from. And I'd keep pushing the union rep to agree rules on new tech before it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of excited, and a bit on edge for the older guys on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, who's 58 and has been framing for 35 years. He's brilliant with his hands but he won't touch a tablet. If the job turns into checking screens, Pete gets pushed out, and that's not fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're adaptive, but your savings are thin. Does that worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If they shuffle the crew and I lose a month, I'm in trouble. That's why I'd rather move up inside Northbeam than jump to something new.

say: AI is a **chance** if workers **share** in the gains.
The technology isn't the enemy; the **deal** with workers is.
think: Being comfortable with **tools** puts him ahead of most on site.
Cuts to **planners** would push site crews to fit panels faster.
do: Volunteer for Northbeam's **AI planning trial** as the site voice.
Take an online course in **building information modelling**, the 3D plans builders use.
Push the union rep for **rules on new tech** before it lands.
feel: **Excited**, and on edge for older crewmates like **Pete**.
S1.quote: I use AI every day to check drawings, and I still want a union in the room when the boss buys the robots.
fieldNote: Combines daily **AI use** with strong **union** loyalty, an unusual mix.
His own job looks safe for now, so **uneasy**, but he worries for **older crewmates**.
Prefers to **move up inside** the firm because savings can't cover a gap.

steps.text: Volunteer for Northbeam's AI planning trial on site
Take an online course in building information modelling
Push the union rep for rules on new site technology

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028 for AI, 2031 for robots that can stand a panel up as well as me. That's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a huge public response, like retraining paid at full wages and the firms sharing what they save. I'd be loud about it in the union. I'd also say on site, learn the machines now, don't wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my site job's gone by 2031. Two years means I'd be learning to fix the robot that replaces me, and I'd be grateful for the chance. The thinking part of my job, like checking drawings, goes in 2028, but the lifting and bolting gives me about three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into the Northbeam factory as soon as I could, in the first six months, and get on the robot maintenance side. I'd do any short course on robot servicing going, nights if I have to. I'd cut my spending hard, no holiday, sell my motorbike, so I've got two months saved when the shake-up comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, really nervous, but not frozen. I'd be busy, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your housemates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One's a delivery driver and one works in a call centre, so they'd be hit before me. I'd tell them to start learning something now, even if it's just how to use the AI they'll be up against. We'd probably end up sharing one cheaper flat for longer than we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would robot maintenance still be a job after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, yeah, until they fix themselves. Nobody knows how long that is. But I'd rather ride that wave than stand on site waiting to be told to go home.

say: The response needs **full-wage retraining** and firms **sharing savings**.
Site workers should **learn the machines** now, not wait.
think: Expects his **site job** to be gone by **2031**.
Drawing checks go in 2028, but **hands-on work** gives about three more years.
do: Move into the Northbeam factory's **robot maintenance** side within six months.
Take any short **robot servicing** course, at night if needed.
Sell his **motorbike** and skip a holiday to save two months' costs.
feel: Really **nervous**, but **not frozen**, because being busy helps.
S2.quote: Two years means I'd be learning to fix the robot that replaces me, and I'd be grateful for the chance.
fieldNote: Expects to lose his site job but has a **clear plan**, so **anxious** rather than alarmed.
Uses the **three-year gap** before robots as his window to switch.
Worries more for **housemates** in driving and call centre work.

steps.text: Move to the Northbeam factory's robot maintenance team
Take a night course in servicing building robots
Sell the motorbike and skip this year's holiday
Push the union for full-wage retraining for site crews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, 2031 and then robots by 2034. Same thing, more room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if we use it, and I'd keep saying the workers should get a share. I'd tell the apprentices on site to learn the robot side now. Online I'd be the annoying guy posting course links.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is long enough to switch from bolting panels together to keeping the panel robots running. I'd be 34 when the robots arrive, still young enough to change. The risk is the money in between, because courses cost and I've got nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd apply for Northbeam's factory apprenticeship in robotics and automation, even at a pay cut for a while. I'd take extra weekend work fixing fences to cover the drop. And I'd keep using AI to study, because it's like a tutor in my pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a knot about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A pay cut with three weeks' rent saved. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight, really tight. I'd probably move to a box room in the flat and pay less. My mum would say come home, but that's two hours away from the factory, so no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Pete in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That he's got a few years to see it coming, and he'd be near retirement by 2034 anyway. I'd still try to get him on a course. He'd tell me to get lost, probably.

say: Five years is a **gift** if workers use it and get a **share**.
Apprentices should learn the **robot side** now.
think: Five years is enough to switch from **bolting panels** to keeping **robots running**.
The risk is **money** in between, since courses cost and he has little saved.
do: Apply for Northbeam's **factory apprenticeship** in robotics, even at a pay cut.
Take **weekend fencing** jobs to cover the drop in pay.
Move into the **box room** to pay less rent.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to switch from bolting panels together to keeping the panel robots running.
fieldNote: Extra time lets him **retrain properly**, but the **pay cut** worries him.
Still **anxious** because thin savings make the switch risky.
Refuses to move home, putting **being near the work** first.

steps.text: Apply for Northbeam's factory apprenticeship in robotics
Fix fences at weekends to cover the apprentice pay drop
Move into the flat's box room to cut rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036 and 2039. I'd be nearly 40. That's loads of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means no excuses for governments or firms. If people end up out of work in 2039, it's because someone didn't plan. I'd say that at union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is enough time to make the change, as long as I don't spend all of it getting comfortable. My worry is me, not the robots. Ten years is long enough to talk myself into waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set myself a deadline, factory or robotics training started within two years. I'd save properly, aiming for three months' rent by 2028. And I'd keep pushing the union to set up a training fund with the builders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. Like I've been given a map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a two-year deadline if you've got ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the people who move first get the good spots. By year eight everyone's trying to get into robot maintenance. I want to be the one training them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about this that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every new gadget makes the boss richer and my rent stays the same. I want my share of what the robots earn. That's the bit I'd fight about.

say: Ten years leaves **no excuses** for governments or firms.
Anyone out of work in 2039 means someone **didn't plan**.
think: Ten years is enough to **make the change** if he doesn't get comfortable.
His main risk is **himself**, not the robots.
do: Push the union for a **training fund** with builders.
feel: Fairly **calm**, like he's been given a **map**.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time to make the change, as long as I don't spend all of it getting comfortable.
fieldNote: A decade plus adaptability makes the future feel **manageable**, so **uneasy**, not anxious.
Sets a **two-year deadline** to beat the crowd into robotics.
Still angry about **who gains** from automation.

steps.text: Start robotics maintenance training within two years
Push the union to set up a builder-funded training fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots arrive while I'm still broke. What would help is being paid while I retrain, and firms that buy robots putting money into training the people they replace.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who gets the money. Every new gadget makes the boss richer and my rent stays the same. I want my share of what the robots earn.

headlineQuote: Every new gadget makes the boss richer and my rent stays the same. I want my share of what the robots earn.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old timber-frame carpenter** fitting factory-built panels on housing sites.
He uses **AI every day** and is a loyal **union** member who wants workers to share the gains.
With about **three weeks' rent** saved, he can't afford a gap while he switches jobs.
In every AGI picture he plans to move into **robot maintenance** at the panel factory.
His mood stays **uneasy to anxious**, because he has a plan but little money.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots arrive by 2031 while he still has no savings.
whatWouldHelp: Being **paid** while retraining, funded by firms that buy **robots**.
